procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated January 20-21, 1965, in Income-tax Reference No. 67 of 1961.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Bombay High Court issued a judgment and order in Income-tax Reference No. 67 of 1961 on January 20-21, 1965.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Both the Commissioner of Income-tax and the assessee (CIBA of India Ltd.) appealed the High Court's decision to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court heard Civil Appeals Nos. 9 to 16 of 1967. The Supreme Court dismissed all appeals with costs.

directions: Both the sets of appeals fail and are dismissed with costs.
One hearing fee in each set.

issue.issue_text: Whether the payment made to recoup another person for expenditure on scientific research is an admissible deduction under s. 10(2)(xii) of the Income-tax Act, 1922.

facts: The assessee made payments to another person (a Swiss company) to reimburse them for scientific research expenditure that the other person had incurred.
law: For an expense to be an admissible deduction under s. 10(2)(xii) of the Income-tax Act, 1922, the expenditure must be laid out or expended *by the assessee* on scientific research related to their business.
application: The Supreme Court found that the assessee did not directly spend the money on scientific research.
Instead, the assessee's payment was merely to 'recoup' or reimburse the other person for research that person had already conducted.

The court reasoned that unless the research is carried on *for* or *on behalf of* the assessee, simply reimbursing another party for their research costs does not qualify as the assessee itself expending money on research.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the claim because the payment was not an expenditure 'laid out or expended on scientific research' by the assessee, but was a reimbursement to another person for research they had conducted. Therefore, it did not meet the specific conditions of s. 10(2)(xii).

issue.issue_text: Whether the payment made for meeting the expenses of Suit No. 890 of 1946 is an allowable expense under s. 10(2)(xv) of the Income-tax Act, 1922.

facts: Suit No. 890 of 1946 was filed before the assessee company was registered or came into existence.
The assessee later made a payment to the Swiss Company to cover a share of the costs incurred in that lawsuit.
law: For an expense to be allowable under s. 10(2)(xv) of the Income-tax Act, 1922, it must be laid out or expended wholly and exclusively for the purpose of the assessee's own business.
application: The Court reasoned that since the lawsuit was initiated before the assessee company was even registered, the assessee had no trading interests to protect at that time.
Therefore, when the assessee later paid for the costs of that pre-existing lawsuit, it was not an expenditure made to protect its own business or trading interests.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the payment for the expenses of Suit No. 890 of 1946 was not an allowable expense because the suit was filed before the assessee company existed, and thus the payment was not made to protect its own trading interests as required by the Act.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the payment made for meeting the expenses of Suit No. 890 of 1946 is an allowable expense under s. 10(2)(xv) of the Income-tax Act, 1922.
appellant_arguments: The payment was made to protect the assessee's trading interests, as it was entitled to the rights of the patents being defended in the suit through its agreements with Ciba (India) Ltd. and the Swiss Company.

Alternatively, the obligation of the Swiss Company to pay for the suit was a debt that Ciba (India) Ltd. was liable to discharge, and this liability was transferred to the assessee under their agreement of June 18, 1948.
respondent_arguments: The assessee was not protecting its trading interests because the suit was filed before the assessee company was registered.
It was not proven that the obligation of the Swiss Company to pay a share of the costs was transmitted to the assessee.
The agreement only required the assessee to pay the debts and liabilities of Ciba (India) Ltd., not those of the Swiss Company.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A question or argument that was not advanced before the Tribunal or departmental authorities cannot be investigated for the first time in the High Court.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court disallowed the deduction of legal costs paid by the assessee for a patent infringement suit because the assessee had no legal rights to the patents being defended, the suit was initiated before the assessee company was even registered, and the assessee had not contractually assumed the specific liability for these costs. The court found that the payment was not made to protect the assessee's own trading interests.
legal_tests_applied: To determine if an expense is an allowable deduction under s. 10(2)(xv), the court examines whether the expenditure was incurred for the purpose of the assessee's business. This involves a factual and contractual analysis of the assessee's legal interest in the subject of the expense and whether a legal obligation existed for the assessee to make the payment.
why_appellant_lost: The assessee failed to prove it had any rights to the specific patents for 'sulphathiazole' or 'thiazamide' that were the subject of the lawsuit; the agreement with the Swiss Company did not grant the assessee rights to those particular patents obtained from May and Baker.
The lawsuit (Suit No. 890 of 1946) was filed before the assessee company was registered, which undermines the claim that the payment was made to protect its own trading interests.

The assessee did not prove that the Swiss Company's obligation to pay the legal costs was ever transmitted to Ciba (India) Ltd. Therefore, the liability did not devolve upon the assessee under its agreement, which was only to assume the debts and liabilities of Ciba (India) Ltd., not those of the Swiss Company.
why_respondent_won: The terms of the agreement between the assessee and the Swiss Company clearly showed that the assessee's patent rights did not include the specific patents at issue in the lawsuit.
The timing of the lawsuit, which predated the assessee's incorporation, demonstrated that the assessee was not protecting its own existing business interests by making the payment.

The assessee's contractual obligation was limited to the debts of Ciba (India) Ltd., and it was not established that the Swiss Company's liability for the suit costs had ever become a liability of Ciba (India) Ltd.
